title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
extended_summary:
This review examines how teachers support students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) in classroom practice. The paper asks two broad questions: how teachers attempt to promote SRL, and what is known from classroom observation studies about the relationship between those practices and student outcomes. The authors distinguish between direct promotion of SRL through explicit strategy instruction and indirect promotion through learning environments that require students to regulate their own learning.

The paper does not test a new intervention. Instead, it synthesizes 17 classroom observation studies published between 1990 and 2019, drawing on research conducted in primary and secondary school settings across several countries. The reviewed studies involve teachers and students in subjects such as mathematics, writing, physics, and mixed subject areas. The authors use this evidence to build a framework contrasting explicit strategy instruction, implicit strategy instruction, and indirect activation of SRL through constructivist and autonomy-supportive learning environments.

The main conclusion is that teachers in typical classrooms spend relatively little time on explicit metacognitive strategy instruction, although some classrooms do provide learning environments that indirectly encourage SRL. The review argues that effective support for SRL requires explicit teaching of strategies, including explanations of what to do, when, why, and how, alongside opportunities for reflection and practice. It also concludes that classroom observation should be complemented with teacher and student self-report when studying SRL practice, because observations capture overt behavior but not teachers’ intentions or students’ internal regulation processes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conceptual/systematic review of classroom observation studies, but it is not a meta-analysis or a primary causal study. Its evidence base is observational and heterogeneous, so it meets only limited credibility criteria for causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for K-12 instructional practice and baseline coaching design, but it does not estimate a causal effect of a specific intervention. Its impact is therefore conceptual and moderate rather than demonstrably large or directly measurable.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual review of 17 classroom-observation studies on teachers’ support for self-regulated learning (SRL), not an intervention effect study. Across the reviewed studies, teachers typically provided very little explicit strategy instruction; for example, suggestions for strategy use were reported in only 2.28% of observation intervals in one study (Moely et al., 1992), and explicit strategy teaching was rare overall. The review argues that explicit instruction, metacognitive reflection, and supportive learning environments are the key baseline/non-AI mechanisms for improving students’ metacognition and SRL.
finding.measure: Classroom observation ratings of direct/indirect SRL support; teacher/student ratings; student self-reported strategy use and achievement where reported in the reviewed studies
finding.study_size: n=541 teachers; n=2318 students across 17 studies reviewed

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes evidence that when teachers explicitly address metacognitive strategies, students’ strategy use and sometimes performance improve, but the paper itself does not report a new pooled effect size. In the included studies, explicit instruction was associated with better performance in one study (Kistner et al., 2010), while another study found no difference in mathematics progress despite more regular and explicit strategy promotion, though students’ metacognitive strategy use increased over time (Depaepe et al., 2010).
finding.measure: Observed direct strategy instruction; student performance in mathematics; student metacognitive strategy use
